section_summary: This section examines Japan’s 1934 Petroleum Industry Law and its effects on foreign oil companies, especially compulsory reserves, sales quotas, licensing, prices, and refinery plans. Embassy reports and company correspondence describe protests by American, British, and Netherlands interests, while State Department memoranda consider coordinated representations and possible restrictions on oil exports to Japan. The section also contains industry statistics and a translated Soviet article on Japan’s fuel supply.

subfiles.title: Discussion of the Oil Industry Law
subfiles.doc_type: article or explanatory paper, concluding pages
subfiles.about: Explains reserve-stock schedules, government oversight, and the law’s place in a controlled economy.
subfiles.summary: The concluding pages calculate when importers and refiners must begin holding petroleum reserves and describe powers to regulate prices and facilities. They explain the advisory role of the Oil Industry Committee and argue for state guidance of economic activity.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning enforcement of the Petroleum Industry Law
subfiles.to: J. C. Goold, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Clarifies existing importers’ licenses and the annual approval of petroleum sales plans.
subfiles.summary: Fukuda says existing importers may continue operating, while approved annual business plans will set sales quantities.

subfiles.title: Protest against revised gasoline sales allotment
subfiles.from: J. C. Goold, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.to: Machida Chuji, Minister of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.about: Protests Standard-Vacuum’s gasoline allotment and the cost and risk of mandatory reserves.
subfiles.summary: Goold argues that the revised allotment denies the company a share of growing demand. He says it will comply with reserve requirements only if the government funds storage and stocks and covers losses and expenses.

subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Minister’s response to petroleum representations
subfiles.about: Reports the Foreign Minister’s response to an oral U.S. message on foreign oil companies.
subfiles.summary: The minister acknowledged the companies’ uncertainty and the hardship of costly storage without assurance of future business.

subfiles.title: Notice to London of Tokyo petroleum conversation
subfiles.about: Relays Neville’s report and directs confidential oral notice to the British Foreign Office.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards the Japanese minister’s response and asks the Embassy to inform the Foreign Office confidentially.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Walter C. Teagle
subfiles.about: Records notice to Teagle of U.S. representations in Tokyo and a discussion of related oil matters.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck tells Teagle of the informal approach to Japan and requests discretion. They also discuss British action, oil-company difficulties in Canton, and a forthcoming meeting.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Surveys diplomatic protests and the commercial effects of Japan’s petroleum controls.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports British and Netherlands representations, Japanese Foreign Office doubts about compulsory storage, and foreign companies’ reluctance to submit binding investment plans. He discusses possible refinery licenses, newspaper criticism, attempts to limit crude-oil supplies to Manchuria, and a reported plan to reduce foreign firms’ market shares gradually.

subfiles.title: Netherlands aide-mémoire on petroleum regulations
subfiles.about: Requests relief from provisions that threaten Netherlands oil interests in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Netherlands Legation cites costly reserve stocks, uncertain annual licenses, refinery policy, and government price controls. It asks Japan to remedy conditions that prevent Rising Sun and associated Netherlands interests from making secure investment decisions.

subfiles.title: British aide-mémoire on petroleum legislation
subfiles.about: Seeks clarification and discussion before British firms commit capital to storage and refining.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy says British importers face imminent decisions on tanks and possible refineries without assurance of future licenses or trade volume. It requests discussion and explicit assurances under the new law.

subfiles.title: Neville–Kurusu interview on oil controls
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s concerns about storage rules and possible foreign retaliation.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu calls the storage requirement impracticable and seeks assurances for foreign firms while warning of possible oil-export restrictions.

subfiles.title: Renewed British representations on Japan’s petroleum law
subfiles.about: Reports the British Ambassador’s October 5 aide-mémoire seeking modification of the law’s operation.
subfiles.summary: Neville relays British concern that firms lack assurances needed to submit complete 1935 plans and avoid hardship.

subfiles.title: Forwarding of British petroleum representations
subfiles.about: Forwards Neville’s report of renewed British representations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department transmits the substance of the October 5 British aide-mémoire to London.

subfiles.title: British Foreign Office consultations on Japanese petroleum law
subfiles.from: H. C. Millard, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Reports oral exchanges with the British Foreign Office about petroleum representations.
subfiles.summary: Millard says the Foreign Office was informed of U.S. messages and instructed its ambassador in Tokyo to make further representations.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Deterding and Teagle
subfiles.about: Records oil executives’ proposals for joint protest and possible restrictions on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Teagle and Deterding describe the law as threatening their Japanese businesses and propose coordinated government protest and a U.S. inquiry into oil-export restrictions. Phillips arranges a meeting with Interior Secretary Ickes.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Industry Control Law, Japanese Empire
subfiles.about: Sets out the company’s account of Japanese oil controls and projected costs.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces price controls and gasoline competition before describing the 1934 law’s licensing, business-plan, and reserve-stock requirements. It estimates large storage and inventory costs, questions the economics of a Japanese refinery, and says the company would require government funding and indemnity to comply with compulsory reserves.

subfiles.title: Japan–Korea–Formosa deliveries into consumption, 1930–1933
subfiles.about: Compares petroleum-product deliveries and market shares by company and year.
subfiles.summary: Tables list product volumes and market shares across Japan, Korea, and Formosa for 1930–1933.

subfiles.title: Japan territory investment and business figures
subfiles.about: Tabulates investments, depreciated values, receivables, and sales for Japanese territories.
subfiles.summary: The tables summarize property values, inventory, accounts, and sales for Yokohama, Keijō, Formosa, and totals.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing article on Japan’s fuel program
subfiles.about: Sends a translation of a newspaper article discussed at a meeting.
subfiles.summary: The writer encloses a translated article containing information on Japan’s fuel program.

subfiles.title: Japan’s fuel base
subfiles.about: Assesses Japan’s domestic fuel resources, oil dependence, concessions, and synthetic-fuel efforts.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that Japan’s growing oil demand far exceeds domestic production and surveys coal, hydropower, colonial sources, North Sakhalin concessions, and foreign imports. It describes exploration in Manchuria, shale-oil production at Fushun, coal hydrogenation, strategic reserves, and the difficulty of sustaining wartime fuel supplies under blockade.

subfiles.title: Internal discussion of proposed petroleum action
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Considers the oil executives’ proposal and who should initiate joint government action.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck questions whether Deterding seeks U.S. leadership despite larger British-Dutch interests. Participants favor considering action if Britain and the Netherlands initiate it.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck’s preliminary conversation with Ickes
subfiles.doc_type: memorandum of conversation, with duplicated opening page
subfiles.about: Records Hornbeck’s briefing of Ickes before the meeting with oil executives.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck explains the State Department’s preference for British or Netherlands initiative and suggests questions Ickes should ask Teagle and Deterding. Pages 445 and 446 repeat the opening page.

subfiles.title: Conference with Ickes, Deterding, and Teagle
subfiles.about: Records a discussion of Japanese oil controls and possible coordinated restrictions on crude-oil exports.
subfiles.summary: Teagle and Deterding explain why price and reserve provisions threaten their Japanese operations and propose surveying and restricting U.S. crude-oil exports. Ickes considers the proposal practical, but Hornbeck says Britain and the Netherlands should initiate any joint government action. The participants discuss a written approach through London.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Netherlands Legation representative
subfiles.about: Records a Netherlands inquiry about the U.S. response to Japan’s petroleum law.
subfiles.summary: Molekamp conveys his government’s readiness in principle to make representations. Hamilton says the United States regards company objections as well founded and would consider British and Netherlands proposals for joint or concurrent action.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Walter C. Teagle
subfiles.about: Updates Teagle on the absence of a British proposal concerning Japanese petroleum controls.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says the Department remains concerned and awaits a British initiative; Teagle says the companies are anxious.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Walter C. Teagle on diplomatic action
subfiles.about: Clarifies the U.S. position on proposed British and Netherlands representations.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck tells Teagle that the United States awaits a definite British proposal and corrects apparent misunderstandings in a telegram from Deterding. He reiterates that State is open to considering joint or concurrent action initiated by the British and Netherlands governments. The text ends mid-conversation.
